title: Burns as song-maker: sources and publication
short: Burns reshaped older popular verses into this song, first printed by Pietro Urbani in 1794 and in Johnson's Scots Musical Museum (vol. 5).
body: In his last decade Burns collected, mended and rewrote Scottish songs for James Johnson's Scots Musical Museum and George Thomson's Select Collection. This lyric is a characteristic piece of that work: several of its images and phrases are found in earlier chapbook and broadside songs, including 'The Turtle Dove' and a farewell song printed in garlands, while Burns's achievement is the selection and compression. The song was first printed in Pietro Urbani's Selection of Scots Songs (1794), and then in the fifth volume of the Museum (1797) as no. 402, with an 'Old Set' as no. 403. Burns did not publish it as a 'poem' at all, which is why editors place it among the songs.

title: a red, red rose
short: The doubled adjective, a folk-song habit, intensifies the colour and the feeling; the rose stands for beauty at its freshest.
body: Repetition such as 'red, red' is a mark of oral song rather than literary poetry, and it gives the line its emphatic, unsophisticated warmth. Very similar opening lines are found in older popular songs; one late-seventeenth-century broadside has a closely parallel first stanza. The rose as an emblem of beauty and love is ancient, and its usual companion idea, that roses fade, is quietly present: the rose is 'newly sprung', and the song's later vows set permanence against time.

title: newly sprung in June
short: The rose has just bloomed: the beloved and the love are at their first freshness.
body: 'Sprung' is the past participle of 'spring', to grow or come up. June is the season of roses in Scotland. The detail is simple, but the word 'newly' matters: it makes the comparison about a beginning, which the rest of the song then tries to extend to the end of time. Compare the double sense in the next simile, where love is like a melody that exists only while it is being played.

title: like the melodie ... sweetly play'd in tune
short: A song that compares love to a song: the lyric draws attention to its own music.
body: The second simile turns from sight to sound. The song was written to be sung, and its tune history is complicated. Burns asked Johnson to set it to Niel Gow's strathspey 'Major Graham', and the Museum printed it so; Thomson later used a different air. The tune now usual, 'Low Down in the Broom', was attached to it in R. A. Smith's Scotish Minstrel (1821) and made the song world-famous. Kirsteen McCue has argued that the choice of melody materially changes how the words are heard.

title: Stanza and metre
short: Four quatrains in ballad or common measure: alternating lines of four and three stresses, rhyming abcb.
body: The song uses the commonest metre of British popular song and hymn, the ballad quatrain (8.6.8.6 syllables, with variations). Only the even lines rhyme ('June'/'tune', 'I'/'dry'). The switch from third person ('my Luve's like') to direct address ('As fair art thou') in this stanza turns the song into a vow spoken to the girl. The comparisons 'As fair ... / So deep' balance her beauty and his love.

title: bonie
short: Scots 'bonie' (bonny): pretty, fair, attractive; 'lass' is a girl or young woman.
body: Burns's own preferred spelling is 'bonie' with one n. The word probably comes from French bon, bonne, 'good', and became a key word of Scots love-song. It is the only Scots word in this line, and the song as a whole is in a light Scots that English singers could manage easily, which helped its wide circulation. In this song it is one of a handful of Scots markers ('a'', 'gang', 'weel', 'o'') that keep the lyric recognisably Scottish without making it hard for non-Scots singers. Burns's other songs use the word constantly ('Ye banks and braes o' bonie Doon').

title: Luve / luve
short: Scots spelling of 'love'; in the song it means both the beloved person ('my Luve') and the feeling ('so deep in luve').
body: The spelling reflects Scots pronunciation, closer to 'lyuv'. Many printings capitalise 'Luve' when it means the beloved and not when it means the passion, as this text does. Readers have noticed that the opening similes could therefore apply either to the girl or to the speaker's love itself; the second stanza resolves it by addressing 'thou', but the ambiguity gives the opening its generality.

anchor: Till a’ the seas gang dry
title: Till a' the seas gang dry
short: 'Until all the seas go dry': a vow of love lasting until an impossible event.
body: 'A'' is 'all' and 'gang' is 'go'. The figure is adynaton, the rhetorical naming of an impossibility to express forever, which is common in popular love songs and farewell songs. Similar vows appear in the older broadside material Burns drew on. The line is then repeated at the start of stanza 3. The vow's grandeur is deliberately out of proportion to the simple speaker, a familiar effect of folk song, where ordinary lovers swear by the whole world. It also introduces the theme of time and change that runs through the rest of the song.

anchor: Till a’ the seas gang dry
title: Repetition across stanzas
short: The last line of stanza 2 becomes the first of stanza 3, a linking repetition typical of song.
body: This device, repeating the end of one unit at the beginning of the next (anadiplosis), gives the song its incantatory force and also suits singing, where the repeated words can carry the melody. 'I will luve thee still, my dear' recurs as well (ll. 7, 11). The refrain-like repetitions make the vow sound as if it is being sworn again.

title: the rocks melt wi' the sun
short: A second impossibility: until the sun melts the rocks.
body: The image heightens the first vow by adding a cosmic heat to the drying seas. The older broadside 'The Turtle Dove' and related songs have similar lines about seas going dry and rocks melting. Burns keeps the folk idiom but makes the stanza more compact. 'Wi'' is 'with'. The cumulative structure (seas, rocks, sands) moves from water to stone to the grains of time, each image a little more intimate, until the vow reaches the length of a human life. Groups of three impossibilities are easy to remember and common in popular verse.

title: the sands o' life
short: The sand of an hourglass, an old image of the time a life has left to run.
body: After two images of the end of the world, the third vow is about the length of the lover's own life. The hourglass emblem of mortality was a commonplace in eighteenth-century writing and church art. 'While the sands o' life shall run' therefore admits a limit that the hyperboles deny, giving the vows a human measure. The image may also recall the sands of the seashore, linking it with the 'seas' of the preceding lines.

title: fare-thee-weel ... a while
short: The song becomes a parting song: the lover is going away and promises to return.
body: 'Weel' is 'well'. The last stanza reveals the situation: the vows are a leave-taking. 'A while' insists that the separation is temporary. Parting songs of soldiers and sailors were a staple of the broadsides Burns knew, and the hyperbolic last line belongs to that tradition. The repetition of 'fare-thee-weel' and of 'my Luve' gives the stanza the sound of a refrain. Some readers find the sudden revelation of departure a little abrupt, a sign of the song's patchwork origins; others feel that it explains, after the event, the extravagance of the vows that precede it.

title: ten thousand mile
short: A stock phrase of farewell ballads; 'mile' as plural is normal in Scots and in folk speech.
body: The phrase is found in the older song 'The Turtle Dove' and related broadside farewells, which Burns knew. Using 'mile' without -s after a number is standard in Scots and in many English dialects. The exaggerated distance mirrors the exaggerated time of the earlier vows and ends the song on the promise of return. The song thus closes on a borrowed phrase, a sign of its place in a shared tradition rather than a lapse in originality.
